claim: Cancer patients show increased morbidity with COVID-19.
source: Cancer patients show increased morbidity with COVID-19 and need effective immunization strategies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background statement and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Many healthcare regulatory agencies recommend administering 'booster' doses of COVID-19 vaccines beyond the standard two-dose series for cancer patients.
source: Many healthcare regulatory agencies recommend administering 'booster' doses of COVID-19 vaccines beyond the standard two-dose series, for this group of patients.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about regulatory recommendations.

claim: A third dose of COVID-19 vaccine leads to seroconversion in 57% of patients that were seronegative after primary vaccination series.
source: We demonstrate that a third dose of COVID-19 vaccine leads to seroconversion in 57% of patients that were seronegative after primary vaccination series.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results section.

claim: The immune response to the third dose is durable as assessed by anti-SARS-CoV-2 (anti-S) antibody titers, T-cell activity, and neutralization activity against wild-type (WT) SARS-CoV2 and BA1.1.529 at 6 months of follow-up.
source: The immune response is durable as assessed by anti-SARS-CoV-2 (anti-S) antibody titers, T-cell activity, and neutralization activity against wild-type (WT) SARS-CoV2 and BA1.1.529 at 6 months of follow-up.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by longitudinal data in the results.

claim: A fourth dose of COVID vaccine led to adequate immune boost in 67% of severely immunocompromised hematologic malignancy patients who were unable to mount an adequate immune response (titer <1000 AU/mL) after the third dose.
source: A subset of severely immunocompromised hematologic malignancy patients that were unable to mount an adequate immune response (titer <1000 AU/mL) after the third dose and were treated with a fourth dose in a prospective clinical trial which led to adequate immune boost in 67% of patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from the fourth dose study.

claim: Low baseline IgM levels were associated with inadequate seroconversion after the fourth dose.
source: Low baseline IgM levels and CD19 counts were associated with inadequate seroconversion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Low baseline CD19 counts were associated with inadequate seroconversion after the fourth dose.
source: Low baseline IgM levels and CD19 counts were associated with inadequate seroconversion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Booster doses induced limited neutralization activity against the Omicron variant.
source: Booster doses induced limited neutralization activity against the Omicron variant.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by neutralization assay data in the results.

claim: COVID-19 in patients with cancer carries a higher morbidity and mortality, especially in patients with hematologic malignancies.
source: It is now well established that coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in patients with cancer carries a higher morbidity and mortality, especially in patients with hematologic malignancies (Kuderer et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Mehta et al., 2020; Khoury et al., 2022; Tang and Hu, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Overall case fatality from COVID-19 has decreased over time, mostly related to the impact of broad vaccinations and improved supportive/antimicrobial management.
source: While overall case fatality has decreased over time, mostly related to the impact of broad vaccinations and improved supportive/antimicrobial management, a higher case fatality rate was noted among cancer patients even during the Omicron (B.1.1.529) wave (Lee et al., 2022; Pinato et al., 2022; Bestvina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A higher case fatality rate was noted among cancer patients even during the Omicron (B.1.1.529) wave.
source: While overall case fatality has decreased over time, mostly related to the impact of broad vaccinations and improved supportive/antimicrobial management, a higher case fatality rate was noted among cancer patients even during the Omicron (B.1.1.529) wave (Lee et al., 2022; Pinato et al., 2022; Bestvina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Advanced age, co-morbidities, and performance status have emerged as key factors adversely impacting outcomes among patients with a cancer diagnosis.
source: Advanced age, co-morbidities, and performance status have emerged as key factors adversely impacting outcomes among patients with a cancer diagnosis (Grivas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Patients with hematologic malignancies have lower rates of seroconversion as defined by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike antibody (anti-S antibody) titers despite COVID-19 vaccines inducing high levels of immunity in the general population.
source: However, emerging data suggests that despite these vaccines inducing high levels of immunity in the general population, patients with hematologic malignancies have lower rates of seroconversion as defined by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike antibody (anti-S antibody) titers (Thakkar et al., 2021; Addeo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Specific therapies, such as anti-CD20 antibodies, BTK-inhibitors, and stem cell transplantation (SCT), have an association with lower rates of seroconversion.
source: Evidence has also suggested that specific therapies, such as anti-CD20 antibodies, BTK-inhibitors, and stem cell transplantation (SCT), have an association with lower rates of seroconversion (Schönlein et al., 2022; Guven et al., 2022; Dahiya et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The median age of the third dose study cohort was 68 years (63.25–76.5 years).
source: The median age was 68 years (63.25–76.5 years).
evidence: This is a baseline characteristic reported in the results section.

source: Fifty-five percent (58/106) of patients were female and 45% (48/106) were male.

claim: Sixty-eight percent (72/106) of patients received BNT162b2 as their primary vaccination, 26% (28/106) received mRNA-1273, and 6% (6/106) had received Ad26.CoV2.S.
source: Sixty-eight percent (72/106) received BNT162b2, 26% (28/106) received mRNA-1273, and 6% (6/106) had received Ad26.CoV2.S.

claim: Seventy-four percent of patients (78/106) received a booster BNT162b2 vaccine and 26% (28/106) patients received booster mRNA-1273 vaccine.
source: Seventy-four percent of patients (78/106) received a booster BNT162b2 vaccine and 26% (28/106) patients received booster mRNA-1273 vaccine.
evidence: This is a baseline characteristic reported in the results section.

source: The majority of the patients, 62% (66/106), had a hematologic malignancy and 38% (40/106) had a solid tumor diagnosis.

claim: The majority of patients, 75% (80/106), were being actively treated at the time of receiving the third dose of the vaccine.
source: The majority of patients, 75% (80/106), were being actively treated at the time of receiving the third dose of the vaccine.

source: Thirty-three percent of the patients (35/106) were seronegative after two doses.

claim: At 4 weeks following the receipt of the booster vaccine, 57% (20/35) of seronegative patients seroconverted and had a detectable antibody response.
source: At 4 weeks following the receipt of the booster vaccine, 57% (20/35) of these patients seroconverted and had a detectable antibody response as demonstrated by anti-S antibody testing, meeting the primary endpoint of our study.
evidence: This is a primary outcome reported in the serology results section.

claim: The median titer at baseline (after primary vaccination) for the entire cohort was 212.1 AU/mL (IQR 50–2873 AU/mL).
source: The median titer at baseline (after primary vaccination) for the entire cohort was 212.1 AU/mL (IQR 50–2873 AU/mL) and the median titer at 4 weeks (after third dose of the vaccine) for the entire cohort was 9997 AU/mL (IQR 880.7–47,063 AU/mL) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result reported in the serology results section.

claim: The median titer at 4 weeks (after third dose of the vaccine) for the entire cohort was 9997 AU/mL (IQR 880.7–47,063 AU/mL).
source: The median titer at baseline (after primary vaccination) for the entire cohort was 212.1 AU/mL (IQR 50–2873 AU/mL) and the median titer at 4 weeks (after third dose of the vaccine) for the entire cohort was 9997 AU/mL (IQR 880.7–47,063 AU/mL) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result reported in the serology results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The median rise in anti-S titer for patients with hematologic malignancies was 2167 AU/mL (IQR 0–10,131 AU/mL) versus 31,010 AU/mL (IQR 9531–44,464 AU/mL) in patients with solid malignancies (p<0.001).
source: The median rise in anti-S titer for patients with hematologic malignancies was 2167 AU/mL (IQR 0–10,131 AU/mL) versus 31,010 AU/mL (IQR 9531–44,464 AU/mL) in patients with solid malignancies (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a comparative result with statistical significance reported in the serology results section.

claim: Within the hematologic malignancies, patients with lymphoid cancers had a lower rise in median anti-S titers (1169 AU/mL, IQR 0–8661 AU/mL) compared to those with myeloid malignancies; median anti-S titer 9424 AU/mL (IQR 4381–20,444 AU/mL) (p<0.001).
source: Within the hematologic malignancies, patients with lymphoid cancers had a lower rise in median anti-S titers (1169 AU/mL, IQR 0–8661 AU/mL) compared to those with myeloid malignancies; median anti-S titer 9424 AU/mL (IQR 4381–20,444 AU/mL) (p<0.001) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a comparative result with statistical significance reported in the serology results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Patients on Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor (BTKi) therapy (n=12) had a median rise in anti-S antibody of 0 AU/mL (IQR 0–3393 AU/mL) compared to a median rise of 9355 AU/mL (IQR 877.3–34410 AU/mL) in anti-S antibody for patients not on BTKi (p<0.05).
source: Patients on Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor (BTKi) therapy (n=12) had a median rise in anti-S antibody of 0 AU/mL (IQR 0–3393 AU/mL) compared to a median rise of 9355 AU/mL (IQR 877.3–34410 AU/mL) in anti-S antibody for patients not on BTKi (p<0.05) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a comparative result with statistical significance reported in the serology results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Patients on anti-CD20 antibody therapy (n=25) had a median rise in anti-S antibody level of 0 AU/mL (IQR 0–910.5 AU/mL) compared to a median rise of 12,735 AU/mL (IQR 2842–38,863 AU/mL) in patients that did not receive anti-CD20 antibody therapy (p<0.05).
source: Patients on anti-CD20 antibody therapy (n=25) also had a median rise in anti-S antibody level of 0 AU/mL (IQR 0–910.5 AU/mL) compared to a median rise of 12,735 AU/mL (IQR 2842–38,863 AU/mL) in patients that did not receive anti-CD20 antibody therapy (p<0.05). (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a comparative result with statistical significance reported in the serology results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nine patients had a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection and in this cohort the rise in anti-S titers was higher (median 19,350 AU/mL, IQR 9286–32,151 AU/mL), compared to those who did not have prior SARS-CoV-2 infection with a median anti-S titer rise, 6706 AU/mL (IQR 444.1–33,831 AU/mL).
source: Nine patients had a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection and in this cohort the rise in anti-S titers was higher (median 19,350 AU/mL, IQR 9286–32,151 AU/mL), compared to those who did not have prior SARS-CoV-2 infection with a median anti-S titer rise, 6706 AU/mL (IQR 444.1–33,831 AU/mL) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a comparative result reported in the serology results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The rise in anti-S titer at 4 weeks was higher for patients who received an mRNA-1273 booster compared to BNT162b2 booster; median 31,451 AU/mL vs. 5534 AU/mL, respectively.
source: We also observed that the rise in anti-S titer at 4 weeks was higher for patients who received an mRNA-1273 booster compared to BNT162b2 booster; median 31,451 AU/mL vs. 5534 AU/mL, respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a comparative result reported in the serology results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The observation that the rise in anti-S titer at 4 weeks was higher for patients who received an mRNA-1273 booster compared to BNT162b2 booster was not statistically significant.
source: This observation was not, however, statistically significant.
evidence: This is stated in the serology results section following the comparison of booster types.

claim: The median spike antibody titer for patients <65 years of age was 27,451 AU/mL and the median for patients with age ≥65 years was 6152 AU/mL, which was significant at p value 0.03438.
source: Lastly, we also investigated the association of age with spike antibody response at 4 weeks. The median spike antibody titer for patients <65 years of age was 27,451 AU/mL and the median patients with age ≥65 years was 6152 AU/mL. This result was significant at p value 0.03438.
evidence: This is a comparative result with statistical significance reported in the serology results section.

claim: At baseline (after primary vaccination), 88 patients had evaluable T-cell results and a positive T-cell response against SARS-CoV-2 was seen in 74% (65/88) patients.
source: At baseline (i.e. after primary vaccination), 88 patients had evaluable T-cell results and a positive T-cell response against SARS-CoV-2 was seen in 74% (65/88) patients.

source: Of these 65 patients, 21 patients were seronegative for anti-S antibody at baseline.

source: Of the 15 patients with negative anti-S antibody at 4 weeks, 11 had a positive T-cell response.
evidence: This is reported in the T-cell immune responses section.

source: Fourteen patients who had a negative T-cell assay response at baseline had a positive T-cell response at 4 weeks.

source: Anti-S titer showed a positive correlation with T-cell response at baseline and at 4 weeks for this cohort (p<0.001) (Figure 1G).

claim: At baseline, neutralizing antibodies were detected in 47 of 68 (69%) patients who were seropositive at baseline (after primary vaccination).
source: Neutralizing antibodies were detected in 47 of 68 (69%) patients who were seropositive at baseline (after primary vaccination).

source: The correlation between seropositivity and presence of neutralizing antibodies was statistically significant (p<0.001, Fisher's exact test).
